analysis.one_liner: Clawbacks deferred compensation from executives at companies rescued with federal bailout money.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral; it died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: If a company receives emergency federal help to avoid collapsing, top executives at that company would have to give back, or forfeit, deferred compensation such as bonus packages paid over time, for the three years leading up to the rescue. The bill would also block these executives from deferring further pay until the federal assistance is fully repaid, and it would impose an added 100% tax on compensation kept in violation of these rules. It applied to key employees, directors and officers, and anyone at the company earning over $1 million a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who fund emergency rescues of failing companies would not see federal bailouts flow through to executive pay packages. Workers at rescued firms would gain because executive pay tied to company performance would take a direct hit when their employer needed a public rescue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and workers at rescued firms

how_it_helps.text: Executives covered by the bill would forfeit or repay deferred compensation attributable to services in the 36 months before their employer received extraordinary federal assistance.
Covered executives could not defer any further compensation until the federal assistance was fully repaid to the government.

Executives who kept compensation in violation of the rules would face an additional tax equal to 100% of the non-repaid or improperly deferred compensation, effectively taxing it at up to 100% of its value.

analysis.who_pays: Top executives, board members, and other $1-million-plus employees at companies receiving federal rescue assistance, who would lose deferred pay and face a 100% tax on amounts kept in violation of the rules. Companies would also have to rewrite their deferred compensation plans to include the repayment requirement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Highly paid executives at rescued firms

drawbacks.text: The bill only applies prospectively, to compensation deferred in taxable years after enactment, so it would not claw back pay from past bailouts such as the 2008 financial crisis rescues.

Compensation committees and tax planners would have lead time to restructure deferred compensation before any future rescue, and the bill touches only nonqualified deferred compensation plans, not other forms of executive pay.

Critics of pay clawbacks argue they can make it harder for distressed firms to recruit and retain the leadership needed to turn a company around, which could matter most in the very situation a rescue addresses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is a straightforward taxpayer-protection rule: public rescue money should not flow through to the deferred pay packages of the people whose company failed. Its costs fall narrowly on a small group of highly paid executives at firms that needed a public rescue. Its limits are real — it applies only to future deferred compensation and only to nonqualified plans — but it is a targeted fix rather than a broad intervention.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended, never receiving a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on February 11, 2016, with Sens. Blumenthal and McCaskill as cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.
No further action was recorded: the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The executives, directors, and million-dollar employees at companies that might need future federal rescues keep their deferred compensation without any repayment or clawback rule, and no taxpayers gained the protection the bill would have created.

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it without any vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican cosponsor joined, and the bill never moved past referral in the Republican-controlled Senate.

industries.industry: Executives and directors at large financial firms
industries.note: The bill would claw back deferred pay and impose a 100% tax on compensation kept in violation of its rules when a firm takes a federal rescue. Its defeat left executive pay untouched by bailout conditions.

industries.industry: Deferred compensation plan administrators and tax advisers
industries.note: Plans would have to add bailout-repayment provisions, and advisers would face a new 100% excise regime to manage for affected executives. The bill's failure left current 409A rules in place.
